Eighth grade science · Unit 8.9

Natural Selection & Common Ancestry

You may already have learned in Unit 7.9 that helpful traits spread, and in Unit 8.8 how traits are inherited and mutate. Now put them together: variation + inheritance + selection = evolution, the idea that explains the diversity of life and its relatedness. Darwin spent twenty years collecting evidence before publishing. Check how he did it using Unit 0: How Science Works.

Where we left off: Unit 8.8 showed how traits are inherited and how mutations create new ones, and Unit 7.9 introduced adaptation and fossils. You may already have learned that helpful traits spread. Now we assemble the full theory of natural selection and common ancestry with several lines of evidence.

Concept 1 · How it works

Variation, inheritance, and survival add up

Natural selection needs four things: variation among individuals, traits that are inherited, more offspring than can survive, and traits that make some more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, the population changes.

Living things in a population are not all the same: they vary in size, colour, speed and many other traits, and many of those traits are passed on through genes. Most species also produce more young than the food and space can support, so not all survive. If a trait helps an individual survive and have offspring, that trait becomes more common in the next generation. This process is natural selection, and when it adds up over many generations the population has evolved. Use the beetles to see it happen.

Analogy

A race with a filter

Imagine a hurdle race in which leg length varies from birth. Taller runners clear the hurdle more often, so they are more likely to finish and have children. The next generation starts with more tall runners, not because anyone trained, but because the tall variants survived and reproduced. Where it breaks: the runners do not "try" to evolve, and strength gained by training is not inherited. Selection edits the variation that is already there.

Concept 2 · Evidence in action

Natural selection measured in real time

Peter and Rosemary Grant spent 40 years measuring finches on Daphne Major. After a 1977 drought left only large, hard seeds, birds with deeper beaks survived and had chicks with deeper beaks. Evolution was measured within one lifetime.

In the Galapagos Islands, a small group of related birds called Darwin's finches have beaks of different shapes. A beak is a tool, and its depth (how tall it is from top to bottom) decides which seeds the bird can crack. Big, deep beaks can break large, hard seeds; small, slim beaks work best on tiny, soft ones. The biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant measured the beaks of the medium ground finch on the island of Daphne Major year after year, so they could see whether beak depth changed when food changed.

Analogy

Tools for the job

A tiny seed needs tweezers; a hard seed needs nutcrackers. When only nuts are left, the nutcracker-beaked birds eat.

Concept 3 · Changes over time

Fossils show gradual change

Layers of fossils show transitional forms between groups. Whale ancestors, for instance, were four-legged land mammals that gradually shifted to life in water over about 10 million years. Fossils also show extinction and new species appearing.

A fossil is the preserved trace of a living thing from long ago, usually found in layers of rock. Deeper layers are generally older, so fossils can be lined up in time order. A transitional fossil shows features of an older group and a newer group at once. Whale ancestors are a good example, because the fossils show legs shrinking and the nostrils moving toward the top of the head. Scientists use many dating methods to estimate how old the rock layers are; the ages here are approximate.

Analogy

Flip-book

One page looks the same as the next, but flip through many pages and a figure changes shape. Fossil layers are the pages.

Concept 4 · Related by descent

Body parts and DNA reveal relatives

Homologous structures (the same bones with different jobs, like a human arm, bat wing, and whale flipper) point to a shared ancestor. DNA comparisons and embryos agree with the fossil record: the more recent the shared ancestor, the more similar the DNA.

Two species are related if they share a common ancestor, a species they both descended from. Close relatives split apart recently; distant relatives split long ago. Evidence for this comes from the body (the arm of a human and the flipper of a whale have the same set of bones, called homologous structures), from embryos and from DNA, where relatives have more matching letters. Biologists show these relationships as a branching diagram, a family tree for species.

Diagram

The tree of life

Life is shown as a branching tree: when a population splits, each branch keeps changing on its own, and all branches trace back to shared ancestors. Species at the tips are not "higher" or "more advanced" than ones that look older; "new" does not mean "better", only suited to its own environment. Modern biologists group organisms by shared ancestry (who descended from which common ancestor), not just by how much they look alike.

How to read it: each gold dot is a common ancestor: the population that later split into the branches on its right. Humans and chimpanzees join closest to today, so they share the most recent ancestor and the most similar DNA. Humans and fruit flies join far to the left. Dates are rounded estimates, the tree is not to scale, and no tip is "higher" than another.

Analogy

Family resemblance

Siblings look alike; cousins a bit less; distant cousins even less. DNA differences let us rebuild a family tree for all life.

Concept 5 · Artificial and accidental

Selection we cause on purpose or by accident

Artificial selection: people choose which organisms breed, making dogs, crops, and cattle. Accidental selection: overusing antibiotics kills most bacteria but leaves resistant ones to multiply.

Natural selection is not the only kind. In artificial selection (also called selective breeding), people decide which plants or animals get to reproduce, choosing traits such as sweetness in fruit or a gentle temperament in a dog. Selection can also happen by accident: an antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria, but if a few bacteria happen to resist it, they survive and multiply. Over repeated use, resistant bacteria become common, which is why antibiotics should be used only when needed.

Analogy

Breeding for a goal

Wild mustard became cabbage, broccoli, kale, and cauliflower by picking different parts to breed, over only a few thousand years.

Practical connections

SituationWhy it matters

Real world

One wild plant, many foods

FoodThe part people kept choosing
Cabbage and kaleBigger leaves
Broccoli and cauliflowerThick flower clusters
Brussels sproutsBuds along the stem
KohlrabiA swollen stem

All of these are the same species, a wild cabbage plant, shaped by people choosing which plants made seeds over many generations. That is selective breeding, a kind of biotechnology that is thousands of years old. It works with the variation that already exists and takes many generations. Modern tools such as DNA tests (to find which seedlings carry a useful gene) and gene editing aim at the same goal faster. Unit 8.8 looks at both sides of those newer tools.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A person says: "Giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves, and their babies had longer necks." Explain why this is not how natural selection works, and give the correct explanation.

Show a model answer

Traits acquired during life (stretching) are not inherited. In a population of ancestors, necks varied for genetic reasons. Longer-necked individuals reached more food, survived and had more offspring, passing on the genes for longer necks, so the average neck length rose across generations.

Words to know

evolution
Change in a population's inherited traits over generations.
natural selection
Individuals with helpful traits leave more offspring.
variation
Differences among individuals.
adaptation
A trait that improves survival and reproduction.
common ancestor
An ancestor shared by two or more species.
homologous structure
Similar structure from a shared ancestor.
transitional fossil
Fossil showing features of two groups.
artificial selection
Humans choose which organisms breed.
resistance
Ability to survive a drug or pesticide.
extinction
Disappearance of a species.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $8): colored paper dots on patterned fabric and tweezers (predation game), different tools (tweezers, clothespin, spoon) and seeds, comparison pictures of limbs, a printed phylogenetic tree, dried mustard-family vegetables.

  • Concept 1: Play the camouflage predation game for 5 rounds; graph survivors by color.
  • Concept 2: Use "beaks" (tweezers, spoons, clothespins) to pick up different seeds.
  • Concept 3: Draw the forelimb bones of a human, bat, whale, and cat and color-match them.
  • Concept 4: Build a family tree of vertebrates from DNA similarity numbers.
  • Concept 5: Compare broccoli, cabbage, and kale to see mustard-plant breeding.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Individuals evolve." Populations evolve.
  • "Evolution has a goal." It has no plan, only what works now.
  • "Humans came from chimpanzees." They share a common ancestor.
  • "Evolution is just a theory." A scientific theory is a thoroughly tested explanation.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: emphasize that a scientific theory is supported by many independent lines of evidence (Unit 0): fossils, anatomy, DNA, and observed changes.
